rules.statement: Don't ask to replace a private constructor with a primary constructor when the type keeps the constructor private so that callers must go through a static (often async) factory method; a C# primary constructor takes the type's accessibility and can't be private.
rules.why: A primary constructor can't express a type whose only constructor must be private behind a factory, so the primary-constructor convention keeps the classic constructor in that case.
rules.check: Before reporting a classic constructor as a primary-constructor candidate, check its accessibility and whether a static factory such as `StartAsync`/`CreateAsync` is the only way to build the type; if it is private for that reason, don't report it.

rules.statement: In a Roslyn analyzer's test project, give every exemption branch in the analyzer's logic (for example each kind of in-place write: method call, property assignment, field assignment, increment/decrement, pass by `ref`) its own test that expects no diagnostic, along with a test showing that the non-exempt case is reported.
rules.why: If an untested exemption branch regresses, legitimate code gets reported as an error and builds break with no failing test.
rules.check: For each branch or switch case in an analyzer's exemption/suppression logic that the diff adds or changes, look for a matching test asserting no diagnostic; report branches that only some other branch's test covers.

rules.statement: In a test project, name a test region after the member it covers: `{MethodName} Tests` for a method and `{PropertyName} Property Tests` for a property.
rules.why: The test template uses separate region-name forms for methods and properties, and one naming pattern makes tests easy to find across the suite.
rules.check: Look at `#region` names in test classes. A region for a method should read `X Tests`, and a region for a property (such as `SupportedDiagnostics`) should read `X Property Tests`. Don't suggest the method form for a property.
